transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Start: 15:10 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Jesse (Redwood SE), Lena (Solutions), Alex (Cobalt Eng Lead), Priya (SRE), Marcus (CTO), Dana (Infra)

Summary block (auto): quick notes - want high sustained throughput for batch inference, occasional lat spikes during morning bursts, prefer VPC private deployment with reserved capacity but open to hybrid for cost testing.

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick hello - we'll focus on continuous pipelining and token safeguards - want to make sure we understand your workload shape.
[00:18] Alex: yeah thanks, we have a peaky workload 8-10am and 6-8pm local, so bursts of many small seqs and occasional long seqs (500-1k tokens) from analytics pipelines.
[00:30] Jesse: ok are those long seqs user-facing or internal? that affects latency SLOs and batching decisions.
[00:38] Alex: mostly internal, behind async jobs, but still want predictable P95. small seqs are user chat messages 16-64 tokens.
[00:45] Priya: and network is VPC peering to Redwood Private, encryption in transit, we also have strict egress rules.
[00:52] Samir: great. quick question on current stack: are you running an internal GPU fleet today or purely cloud?
[00:58] Marcus: we have some on-prem for regulated data and a cloud burst pool. ideally Redwood Private in our VPC with reserved nodes for predictable throughput.
[01:06] Jesse: perfect. so two things we usually tune: continuous batching/pipelining behavior and scheduler guardrails like max_num_seqs and per-request token limits.
[01:17] Dana: can you clarify max_num_seqs? we saw it in docs but not sure how it interacts with prefix caching.
[01:24] Jesse: yeah, max_num_seqs is basically the scheduler limit for how many partial sequences the runtime will keep open for packing on GPU. if you set it too high you increase packing density but you can blow memory or raise latency on rare long sequences. also interacts with KV cache because each open seq keeps KV state.
[01:41] Alex: so for our mix - tons of tiny seqs plus occasional 1k token runs - what's the recommended approach?
[01:48] Jesse: we typically recommend adaptive windowing: keep max_num_seqs moderate (32-64) and enable continuous pipelining with a small dispatch delay (10-25ms) so tiny requests get batched quickly but long sequences don't hold up the pipeline. we also recommend token caps per-route - e.g., 1024 for analytics route, 256 for chat route.
[02:10] Samir: also leverage KV cache warmstarts for repeated prefixes - that will reduce token work for the chat route and lower per-token cost. but you need a higher eviction threshold to avoid thrashing with your bursty traffic.
[02:25] Priya: what metrics should we monitor to detect thrashing?
[02:29] Jesse: primary ones: kv_cache_hit_rate (per-model, per-tenant), open_seq_count, avg_batch_size, tokens_per_second, and the scheduler queue age. if kv hit rate drops below ~60% during bursts, that's a sign of eviction churn.
[02:44] Alex: ok, that aligns with what we saw. our current kv hit-rate is noisy and drops during peak.
[02:50] Lena: small note, sometimes the transcription of our tests shows k-v cash in logs, so be careful when searching.
[02:57] Samir: ha noted. on quantization, there's tradeoffs: int8 or q4/ q4m can boost throughput 1.5-2x but you may see slight quality differences on completions for long context. for internal analytics that's ok but for chat we might keep float16 or q6 if available.
[03:18] Marcus: would quantized models change scheduler knobs?
[03:22] Jesse: yes slightly - quantized models run faster per-token so you may lower max_num_seqs to avoid GPU saturation; or conversely increase per-GPU concurrency. it's workload dependent; we'll run a perf matrix.
[03:33] Priya: on VPC/on-prem: any extra considerations for cold cache or network lat?
[03:38] Samir: with VPC peering you get predictable network lat but disk-backed KV restores on instance restart can cause cold-cache penalties. we recommend node pinning during pilot and staggered restarts, and enabling local SSD KV snapshots where possible.
[03:54] Dana: can Redwood do the warmstart run with our dataset to simulate morning burst?
[03:58] Jesse: yes we can run kv warmstart with your prefix traces - that's one of the action items. we can also seed the cache and run synthetic replay to measure hit-rates.
[04:09] Alex: questions on token limits: if we set 256 cap for chat route, what happens to requests that exceed?
[04:15] Jesse: depends on policy: you can trim the input, reject with a 413-like error, or route to a fallback model that supports longer contexts but runs on separate pool (higher cost). we often recommend trimming with user notice for chat, and using fallback for analytics.
[04:30] Marcus: fallback route sounds good but we'd want routing policy to prefer cheaper models unless latency impacted. can Redwood support automatic fallback based on queueing?
[04:38] Jesse: yes - smart routing can route by policy: if queue age exceeds threshold or open_seq_count high, route new long requests to a pre-configured fallback pool. that's plumbed in our canary workflows.
[04:48] Samir: one gotcha - in dedicated on-prem pools, cross-pool KV sharing isn't automatic, so fallback may have different cache characteristics. worth simulating.
[04:58] Priya: noted. hearing a lot about evictions - is there a recommended eviction policy setting? LRU vs time-based?
[05:05] Jesse: LRU with a soft TTL works well for bursty user patterns. set soft TTL to retain hot prefixes for the day part. combine with higher kv capacity (if memory allows) and aggressive pre-warming at peak time.
[05:17] Alex: what about continuous pipelining latency impact? when you increase dispatch delay, tiny messages wait longer.
[05:24] Jesse: that's the tradeoff - dispatch delay gives larger batches which improve tokens/sec but increases P50 for small requests. we use dynamic delay: small-request fast-path with low delay, and a slow-path that increases delay for throughput-heavy times.
[05:36] Dana: any examples of exact knobs we should try in pilot? numbers to start with?
[05:40] Jesse: yes. config A (canary): max_num_seqs 32, dispatch_delay 12ms, token_cap_per_request route chat 256, analytics 1024, kv_size_target 60% of memory, eviction LRU softTTL 6h. Config B (HT): max_num_seqs 64, dispatch_delay 20ms, kv_size_target 80%, aggressive quant q4 for analytics, fallback pool enabled.
[06:00] Samir: we'll provide both configs and a benchmarking script. what about observability hooks?
[06:05] Lena: we will add per-route tracing and a dashboard with p50/p95, avg_batch_size, open_seq_count, kv_hit_rate, gpu_util, and a timeline view for evictions. we'll grant your SRE team access to the dashboard.
[06:18] Priya: good - can we get alerts on kv hit-rate drops and open_seq_count spikes?
[06:22] Lena: yep, threshold alerts and automated runbooks.
[06:25] Alex: any limitations for on-prem regarding quantization (licenses or libs)?
[06:29] Jesse: quant kernels sometimes need vendor-specific libs but we can ship compatible runtimes; for air-gapped we produce vetted binaries and test harnesses. there may be small differences in throughput across GPU types.
[06:40] Marcus: about cost - how do we estimate tokens/sec cost if we run HT config vs canary?
[06:45] Samir: we'll share a cost model spreadsheet - cost per token changes with batching because effective tokens/sec increases so per-token infra amortization drops. we'll include examples using your historical token volumes.
[06:58] Dana: timeline - how quickly can we run a pilot?
[07:01] Samir: once we get request traces and IAM access for VPC, we can stand up dedicated nodes and start seeding in ~3-5 business days, run 7-day pilot after.
[07:10] Alex: sounds good. final question - if we hit GPU OOM during test how will rollback work?
[07:15] Jesse: scheduler has guardrails; in case of OOM we auto-throttle new batches and fall back to smaller scheduling window; we also have an emergency cap on open_seq_count to protect nodes. we can also do immediate config rollback via the console.
[07:29] Samir: ok let's recap next steps.
[07:32] Alex: recap would be great.
[07:34] Samir: action items - Jesse to provide two configs and benchmarking scripts; Alex to send request traces and seq histograms; Samir to share cost model and dashboard access. We'll schedule follow-up review the week after pilot ends.
[07:49] Priya: can you email the runbook snippets and the sample alert thresholds?
[07:53] Lena: yes we'll attach them to the calendar invite.
[07:57] Marcus: thanks all.
[08:00] Samir: thanks everyone, we'll send materials by Monday.
[08:04] Meeting end.
